title: Aditya Kher, PhD
text:
I’m an applied physicist and systems engineer experienced in both the quantum and aerospace & defense industries. I’ve spent my career on R&D projects ranging from cryogenic quantum-related technologies to satellite-based remote sensing systems, and have contributed everywhere from experimental and computational research for advanced hardware to rapid development and fielding of operational algorithms. I particularly enjoy mission-oriented technology projects where I can leverage deep physical principles and intuition, whether it’s early-stage R&D or a product that will ship in months.
I developed novel superconducting sensor and amplifier technologies for astronomy instrumentation during my PhD at Caltech, where I was a member of the second cohort of NASA Space Technology Research Fellows and shuttled between campus and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory for my research. Prior to the PhD I received an MS from Caltech and a BS from UC San Diego.
Check out the pages describing my professional work relevant to quantum and defense, as well as my independent projects including a radar detection performance model. You can also take a look at my full CV.
When I’m not working, I’m typically reading The Economist, watching an arthouse film at an independent cinema, or doing some spirited driving in the canyons of Southern California.
Feel free to reach out on LinkedIn or email if you want to talk physics, technology, or movies!

title: Quantum Technology
text:
Transition-edge sensors are a standard detector technology used in modern astronomy instruments, and can also be used as single-photon detectors for quantum information and other applications. A TES is a superconducting bolometer that operates at the edge of the superconducting transition, where its resistance is highly sensitive to changes in temperature. When coupled to an absorber, this makes it an extremely sensitive detector for photons and other particles. Typically, a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device) is used to read out the very small changes in electrical current through the TES that correlate to photon absorption. However, SQUIDs are complex devices, requiring fabrication of multiple layers of superconducting thin films, and they are not straightforward to multiplex. This limits the size of TES arrays, which in turn limits the sensitivity and resolution of instruments that use them.
At Caltech and JPL, I worked under Prof. Jonas Zmuidzinas and Dr. Peter K. Day, who had pioneered a new, highly scalable superconducting detector technology called the microwave kinetic inductance detector (MKID). These are superconducting microwave resonators where the inductance is dominated by kinetic inductance, a property that exists in all conductors but is particularly strong in superconductors. They can be fabricated with a single layer of superconducting material and are straightforward to multiplex, as resonators in a large array can be designed with slightly different resonant frequencies, with the whole array excited and read-out via a frequency comb on a common feedline.






Figure 1: Fabricated KPUP resonator device. Microwave feedline is at the top, and current signal input is coming from the right. Kinetic inductor is towards the bottom of the device, with capacitor comprising most of the device area. Adapted from A. Kher et al., J Low Temp Phys 184, 480–485 (2016).



The group had also been investigating a nonlinearity in the kinetic inductance; namely, that the kinetic inductance has a dependence on the current flowing through the material. For my PhD work, I built on this research and took inspiration from MKID technology in order to develop a novel superconducting current sensor consisting of a microwave resonator with a nonlinear kinetic inductance. This device could be an easily multiplexable alternative to SQUIDs for reading out TESs, which retain some advantages over MKIDs. We named it the kinetic inductance parametric up-converter (KPUP), as it up-converts the low-frequency TES current signal to the microwave domain, where there is much greater available bandwidth for array multiplexing. Like SQUIDs, the added noise from the KPUP, which in principle dissipates no energy, could be quantum-limited.






Figure 2: TES superconducting transition mapped out by KPUP at different temperatures. At low input current, the TES current is equal to the input, and at high input current the TES is ohmic. The transition is in between. Adapted from A. Kher, Dissertation, California Institute of Technology (2017).



I designed and simulated KPUP devices and tested them in a dilution refrigerator with a microwave measurement setup. I measured the device response to DC current bias and observed the expected nonlinear kinetic inductance behavior, and then measured the noise referred to the input signal current, meeting performance benchmarks for TES readout. I then integrated the KPUP with a TES and was able to map the TES superconducting transition by using the KPUP to read out the current through the TES as I varied its temperature. I also demonstrated operation of a KPUP device as a parametric amplifier by applying a strong microwave pump tone and observing almost 30 dB of microwave gain with near-quantum-limited noise. This has applications for superconducting qubit readout as well as in other domains where low-noise microwave amplification is needed.
This work was presented at several conferences and published in the Journal of Low Temperature Physics. A detailed description along with that of a few smaller projects can be found in my PhD thesis.

title: Aerospace & Defense
text:
Figure 1: Illustration of a missile warning satellite. Image1: Lockheed Martin / U.S. Space Force (public domain).



At Northrop Grumman, I worked on the ground system for the US Space Force’s DSP and SBIRS missile warning satellite constellations. Collectively known as Overhead Persistent Infrared (OPIR), these satellites are equipped with infrared sensors that can detect the heat signatures of missile launches from space. The ground system processes the satellite observations in order to identify and track potential missile threats, and to provide early warning to authorities. This data is also used for technical intelligence and situational awareness, and plays a critical role in cueing missile defense systems.
I was part of an R&D team focused on figuring out how to respond to advanced threats. This involved extensive data analysis from the OPIR sensors on threat characteristics, which was then used to inform the development of a real-time, physics-based algorithm to provide warning against these threats. This algorithm incorporated numerical simulation of threat behavior that had to execute in a timely and accurate manner during real-world missile events. An initial version of the algorithm was rapidly developed and deployed to the operational ground system in the span of a year, and after that was continuously improved via model fidelity enhancements and parameter tuning as more event data was collected. Going from research to operations so quickly was a unique and rewarding experience, especially given the critical nature of the application.
This work is now an important part of the national security infrastructure. It was presented at several conferences, winning a Best Poster award at one, and was additionally a key contributor to a $200M+ contract award2.

title: Multistatic Radar Detection Performance Model
text:
This project develops a Python framework for evaluating radar sensor performance against small uncrewed aerial systems (UAS), emphasizing the geometric advantages of multistatic (distributed) configurations over monostatic baselines. The framework implements monostatic and bistatic radar range equations, Shnidman’s detection probability model with Swerling target fluctuation, and an aspect-dependent target radar cross-section model built from composite canonical scatterers and calibrated to published Ku-band small-quadcopter measurements. Outputs include 2D probability-of-detection contours quantifying performance differences between a single monostatic radar and an N-node distributed configuration against low-RCS aspect-dependent targets. The study is motivated by the operational importance of counter-UAS radar and the intuition that geometric diversity in distributed sensor networks provides detection coverage that monostatic systems cannot match, particularly against targets with strong aspect-sensitive RCS suppression.
Project code and reproduction notebook following this study are available.

title: Benchmark Land-Cover Classification on Operational Sentinel-2 Imagery
text:
This project develops a Python framework for applying a benchmark-trained land-cover classifier to arbitrary operational Sentinel-2 scenes and characterizing how its performance degrades away from the benchmark. The framework fine-tunes a pretrained ResNet-18 on the ten-class EuroSAT dataset, then runs the trained model over full Sentinel-2 Level-2A scenes retrieved from Microsoft Planetary Computer: bands are harmonized to the EuroSAT radiometric and spectral convention, tiled into 64×64 chips, classified with per-chip confidence, and reassembled into a georeferenced land-cover map. An independent, physics-based NDVI computation on the same scene provides a second opinion, and the per-chip maximum softmax probability provides an out-of-distribution signal. We apply the framework to two California scenes — a Central Valley agricultural landscape and the Malibu coastline — and use the disagreements among the classifier, the spectral index, and the confidence signal to separate preprocessing (calibration) effects from fundamental limits of benchmark-to-operational transfer. The study is motivated by the gap between benchmark accuracy and operational reliability that governs whether a curated-dataset classifier can be trusted on real sensor feeds.
Project code and a reproduction notebook following this study are available.

title: Benchmark Land-Cover Classification on Operational Sentinel-2 Imagery
text:
This project develops a Python framework for applying a benchmark-trained land-cover classifier to arbitrary operational Sentinel-2 scenes and characterizing how its performance degrades away from the benchmark. The framework fine-tunes a ResNet-18 (Sentinel-2-pretrained) on the ten-class EuroSAT dataset,1 then runs the trained model over full Sentinel-2 Level-2A scenes retrieved from the Microsoft Planetary Computer: bands are harmonized to the EuroSAT radiometric and spectral convention, tiled into 64×64 chips, classified with per-chip confidence, and reassembled into a georeferenced land-cover map. An independent, physics-based NDVI computation on the same scene provides a second opinion, and the per-chip maximum softmax probability provides an out-of-distribution signal. We apply the framework to two contrasting scenes — an agricultural landscape in California’s Central Valley and the Mediterranean coastline near Malibu — and use the disagreements among the learned classifier, the physical index, and the confidence signal to separate preprocessing (calibration) effects from fundamental limits of benchmark-to-operational transfer. The study is motivated by the gap between benchmark accuracy and operational reliability that governs whether a curated-dataset classifier can be trusted on real sensor feeds.
Project code and a reproduction notebook following this study are available.

title: A benchmark classifier meets real sensor data
text:
Two instruments, one scene
The project has two components joined by a single scene-acquisition path. The classifier is a ResNet-18 with Sentinel-2 MoCo-pretrained weights (via torchgeo), fine-tuned on EuroSAT’s ten classes. The vegetation index is NDVI, a fixed physical quantity computed directly on any Sentinel-2 scene retrieved from the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API.
The bridge between them runs the trained classifier over an arbitrary scene: bands are resampled to a common 10 m grid, ordered to match EuroSAT, tiled into 64×64 chips — each covering 640 m on the ground — classified in batches, and reassembled into a georeferenced class map. NDVI provides an independent, physics-based second opinion on the very same pixels.
The design intent is that a learned model and a fixed index are two different instruments looking at the same ground. Where they agree corroborates; where they disagree localizes what each is actually sensitive to. Getting value out of the disagreements, though, requires first ruling out that a disagreement is merely a preprocessing artifact — which is where the calibration layer comes in.

title: A benchmark classifier meets real sensor data
text:
The calibration layer
A preprocessing error looks exactly like a domain-shift finding, so before any scene result can be trusted the pipeline between L1C and L2A has to be right. EuroSAT chips come from L1C products; Planetary Computer serves L2A. Several systematics sit between the two, and most of them the code corrects:

Band order. EuroSAT’s channel order has to be reproduced exactly; a silent permutation would still produce plausible-looking maps. The order is pinned and asserted against the installed torchgeo version.
B10 (cirrus). Present in L1C, consumed by atmospheric correction in L2A. Inference zero-fills that channel; after Normalize(0, 10000) this perturbs one channel by about 0.001 — genuinely mild.
Radiometric offset. L2A processing baseline ≥ 04.00 carries a +1000 DN offset EuroSAT-era data lacks; it is subtracted so the classifier and NDVI see pre-offset values.
Resolution. L2A bands arrive at 10/20/60 m and are resampled onto the 10 m grid of the reference band.

And one systematic the code does not correct, which is the largest of them all. EuroSAT’s L1C is top-of-atmosphere reflectance; L2A is bottom-of-atmosphere (surface) reflectance, with Sen2Cor having removed the atmospheric path radiance the training data still contains. That difference runs to hundreds of DN in the blue and visible bands — one to two orders of magnitude above the B10 effect — and it leaves served scenes darker than the model’s training inputs. Correcting it on-footprint would require L1C for the same scene from a second catalog, which is out of scope here; instead I document it as the leading known systematic and keep it in view when reading every scene result below.
None of this is ceremony. It is the phenomenologist’s habit applied to a machine learning pipeline: name the instrument effects, correct the ones you can, quantify the one you can’t, and only then attribute what remains to the scene.

title: A benchmark classifier meets real sensor data
text:
Scene one: the familiar case
I started where the model should be most comfortable — irrigated agriculture in California’s Central Valley, about the closest thing in North America to the European farmland EuroSAT was built from. Late June, roughly 13 km across.
The class map is coarsely correct: the model calls nearly the whole scene AnnualCrop, with a scattering of HerbaceousVegetation and a few River chips tracing an actual watercourse. NDVI, on the same scene, cleanly separates active from fallow fields — the green fields concentrated on the western side, fallow ground elsewhere.






Figure 1: Central Valley: land-cover class map (left) and NDVI (right). The classifier labels nearly everything cropland; NDVI resolves the active/fallow structure within it.



To compare the two views rigorously they have to live on the same grid, so I aggregated the 10 m NDVI field onto the classifier’s 640 m chips — an operation verified to reproduce the classifier’s own tiling exactly — and grouped the per-chip statistics by predicted class. I went in with two physically-motivated predictions. Both were wrong, and the way they failed is the actual result.

The first prediction was that AnnualCrop would key on field geometry and so span a wide NDVI range including low, fallow values, separating the classes along the greenness axis. The class NDVI means overlap and the scatter shows no clustering, so greenness does not separate the classes. But greenness is doing real work — orthogonally to the labels. The classifier lumps active and fallow fields together as AnnualCrop (land-cover type) while NDVI resolves the active/fallow state within that class. The two instruments are genuinely complementary; the greenness variation simply lives within a class rather than between classes, which is exactly why it never appeared as separation. That is the honest form of the complementarity I was after.
The second prediction was that HerbaceousVegetation would be the model’s dumping ground for spectrally mixed chips and so carry elevated within-chip σ. Its σ (0.089) is if anything below AnnualCrop’s (0.102). The σ column’s one real signal is River (0.175) — water/land edges inside a 640 m chip, the single place internal spread discriminates.






Figure 2: Per-chip NDVI mean versus within-chip σ, colored by predicted class. The two vegetation classes overlap with no clustering; only River separates, on the σ axis.



So what is the AnnualCrop-versus-HerbaceousVegetation split? On this scene it has no correlate in any variable available to me — greenness, within-chip heterogeneity, or spatial position. And it is not the two classes being confused in the ordinary sense: on the in-domain confusion matrix both sit firmly on the diagonal, their errors going to PermanentCrop, Pasture, and Highway — none of which appear here. The model is not mistaking one for the other the way its own confusion structure would predict.
The confidence column resolves it. Maximum softmax probability (MSP) for all three classes sits at roughly 0.38–0.44, far below the high confidence the model reaches on EuroSAT test data. It is not confidently drawing this distinction; it is hedging, HerbaceousVegetation lowest of the three. That points away from a real cue the network is keying on — which it would apply confidently — and toward genuine out-of-distribution arbitrariness: the argmax tipping between two nearby classes on tiles unlike anything in curated EuroSAT.

title: A benchmark classifier meets real sensor data
section: Confidence as a map, and a leak
text:
Confidence as a map, and a leak
Placing the scene’s MSP against the EuroSAT test set makes the domain shift quantitative. The scene’s confidence peaks near 0.35 with a long tail, where the benchmark clusters at high confidence. By a 0.5 threshold most of the scene is low-confidence — the benchmark model is broadly uncertain on real imagery.






Figure 3: Confidence (MSP) on the Central Valley scene against the EuroSAT test set. The scene’s distribution is shifted far to the left.



The low confidence is not uniform, though. The higher-confidence chips tend to sit over the active green fields and thin out across the fallow ground — the same split NDVI drew — so some of the vegetation state the classifier’s label discards leaks back into its confidence. The effect is real but weak: per-chip confidence and per-chip NDVI correlate at only r = 0.21, a spatial tendency more than a clean relationship. The label says one thing everywhere; its uncertainty carries a faint trace of the information the label threw away.






Figure 4: Low-confidence chips hatched on the class map (left) and per-chip confidence against per-chip NDVI (right). Confidence rises weakly with greenness (r = 0.21).

title: A benchmark classifier meets real sensor data
section: Scene two: the exotic case that wasn’t
text:
Scene two: the exotic case that wasn’t
To stress the model I then picked a scene that looks nothing like Europe: the Santa Monica Mountains meeting the Pacific near Malibu — open ocean, the urban ribbon along the Pacific Coast Highway, and Mediterranean chaparral, which I took to be a biome EuroSAT had never seen. I expected the hard case.
It was the easy one.






Figure 5: Malibu coast: true color (left) and class map with low-confidence chips hatched (right). Water goes to Sea & Lake, the hills to Herbaceous Vegetation, both confidently.



The ocean goes confidently and correctly to SeaLake — EuroSAT has that class, so open water is not out-of-distribution. The chaparral goes to HerbaceousVegetation with high confidence — probably correctly, not by luck, for a reason I return to below. The coastal strip picks up Residential and some River. Confidence is high across most of the scene and drops only where it should: the immediate coastline, where 640 m chips genuinely mix water, beach, and built-up land and no single EuroSAT class fits. The scene’s MSP histogram tracks the EuroSAT test set’s shape, where the Central Valley’s sat far to the left.






Figure 6: Confidence on the Malibu scene against the EuroSAT test set. Unlike the Central Valley, it tracks the benchmark.



The reversal is the lesson, and it corrects the intuition that chose the scenes. “California farmland resembles European farmland, so it should be the easy case” reasoned about the wrong kind of similarity — land use. What actually governs transfer is whether individual 640 m chips resemble EuroSAT’s curated, single-cover tiles, and Malibu is closer on at least two counts. Structurally, it resolves into large near-homogeneous blocks — kilometres of uniform ocean, continuous chaparral, a solid urban strip — each of which looks like one clean EuroSAT patch, where the Central Valley resolves into a fine mosaic of small parcels and bare fallow ground. Spectrally, its vegetation may simply be in-distribution: EuroSAT is a European dataset, southern Europe is Mediterranean, and California shares that Mediterranean biome, so the chaparral plausibly resembles training scenes rather than confusing the model — which is why its label is confident and, most likely, right. Two scenes cannot separate the structural contribution from the spectral one; they are confounded here. But either way, land-use familiarity was the wrong axis, and the exotic-looking coast sat closer to the benchmark than the familiar-looking farmland.

title: A benchmark classifier meets real sensor data
section: What survives contact, and what doesn’t
text:
What survives contact, and what doesn’t
Pulling the two scenes together, four things hold up.
The classifier’s coarse calls are reliable. Cropland, water, urban, the dominant vegetation type — it gets these right on both scenes. The benchmark accuracy does mean something operationally, at the level of coarse land cover.
Its fine distinctions do not survive domain shift. AnnualCrop versus HerbaceousVegetation on the Central Valley is ground-arbitrary. This is not a fixable calibration error; it is what a patch classifier does when real tiles land between its training classes.
Confidence behaved sensibly on both scenes. It was low where inputs are genuinely mixed or unfamiliar — the fallow Central Valley mosaic, the immediate coastline, the ground-arbitrary vegetation split — and high where the coarse call is both solid and in-distribution, including the correctly-labelled ocean and chaparral. The standard caveat still holds in principle: MSP measures typicality, not correctness, so a benchmark model can be confidently wrong and MSP will not catch it. But I should be honest that these two scenes did not produce such a case — the confident calls I could check were all reasonable — so that limitation remains a caveat about the method rather than something I observed here. Confidence proved more trustworthy than I expected going in.
The physical index earns its place. NDVI recovers the active/fallow structure the classifier is blind to, and its disagreements with the classifier are informative rather than noise. A learned model and a physical model looking at the same ground is a stronger position than either alone.
Underneath all of it is the calibration/fundamental split. The band-order, B10, and offset systematics are instrument effects I could and did remove; the TOA/BOA shift is one I chose to bound rather than remove. What remains after that bookkeeping — the ground-arbitrary fine label, and transfer governed by chip-level resemblance rather than geography — is the fundamental behavior of the model on operational data. Getting that attribution right is the entire point: without it, a preprocessing bug and a domain limit are indistinguishable, and you learn nothing about either.

title: A benchmark classifier meets real sensor data
text:
Limitations and deliberate omissions

Two scenes, small counts (four River chips on the Central Valley). The claims are scene-specific illustrations, not statistics; the two scenes are chosen to bracket a spectrum, not to sample it. They also confound the drivers of transfer: Malibu is more in-distribution than the Central Valley on at least two entangled axes — chip homogeneity and spectral/biome resemblance — and two scenes cannot separate their contributions.
The TOA/BOA systematic is uncorrected. An on-footprint L1C-versus-L2A ablation (via a second catalog such as Element84 earth-search or the Copernicus Data Space) would let me measure how much of the confidence shift is atmospheric versus structural. I bounded it rather than measured it.
MSP is a top-1 signal. Two-class hedging would show more directly in the top1–top2 margin or predictive entropy; I kept to MSP as the standard baseline and left the richer signals out on purpose.
No retraining or domain adaptation. Fine-tuning on L2A surface reflectance, or on mixed real-scene tiles, is the obvious way to close the gap — and a different project. This one characterizes the benchmark model as-is; adapting it would hide exactly the behavior I wanted to see.
Plain non-overlapping tiling, no quantitative accuracy. A real product would use overlapping chips and a proper reference such as ESA WorldCover; that is the natural next quantitative anchor, noted rather than claimed here.

title: A benchmark classifier meets real sensor data
text:
Reproducing it
The pipeline is a small installable package with a CLI and an executed notebook walkthrough that reproduces both scenes end to end:
eoml-train    --epochs 3
eoml-classify --bbox WEST SOUTH EAST NORTH --datetime 2024-06-01/2024-06-30 --confidence
eoml-ndvi     --bbox WEST SOUTH EAST NORTH --datetime 2024-06-01/2024-06-30
The --confidence flag hatches low-confidence chips on the saved class map and writes a confidence heatmap alongside it. Unit tests run without network or GPU. Full source: github.com/adityakher/eoml.
